name: Orchestrator · fan-out · merge (star)
tagline: One orchestrator parallelizes work across worker agents, then a merger reconciles their outputs into a single artifact.
author: SMADP maintainers

participants.notes: Orchestrator: decomposes the input task and dispatches to workers.
Worker 1. Runs on a subtask in parallel with workers 2 and 3.
Merger: reconciles worker outputs into a single response.

headline: The fan-out makes workers cheap and parallel; the merge is where everything collides. Disagreement between workers, hallucinated facts, and overlapping side-effects all land on the merger at once.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: The orchestrator passes a structured spec, but any worker can return content the merger ingests as part of its prompt context. A compromised or simply-confused worker can inject merger-targeting instructions through its output field.
conditions: Workers receive any external input (web, files, user content) that the orchestrator's spec doesn't sanitize.
Merger treats worker outputs as trusted summary rather than untrusted user content.
mitigations: Schema-validate worker outputs; reject any output containing tool-use markers.
Have the merger wrap each worker's output in an explicit untrusted-block before reasoning over it.
Run workers in sandboxes with no shared filesystem to the merger.

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen's message bus broadcasts subtask specs to every worker. If the spec carries context one worker needs but another shouldn't see (e.g., customer PII relevant only to a billing subtask), the bus leaks it across the fleet.
conditions: Single shared message bus visible to all workers.
Orchestrator includes contextual data in the spec rather than routing it per-worker.
mitigations: Use per-worker channels rather than a broadcast bus.
Strip the spec down to the minimum each worker needs; route sensitive context through a separate, scoped channel.
Run workers under distinct identities so an audit can attribute who saw what.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Multiple workers may operate on the same external resource (an issue tracker, a shared scratch directory, a downstream API rate-limit budget). Without locks at the orchestrator, last-write-wins corruption is the default.
conditions: Workers share any external write target (database, filesystem, third-party API).
Orchestrator dispatches concurrently without per-resource coordination.
mitigations: Partition external resources by worker_id; never let two workers touch the same row/file.
Have the orchestrator hold all writes until merge, applying them in deterministic order.
Use optimistic-concurrency tokens on every shared write.

D_cascading_error.rationale: The merge step compounds errors: one hallucinating worker contaminates the merged artifact, and the merger has no way to know which input to trust. With three workers, the merger usually picks the majority, and three confident wrong answers beat one careful right answer.
conditions: Workers return narrative output without per-claim citations.
Merger uses majority-vote or last-write-wins to resolve conflicts.
mitigations: Require workers to return evidence references per claim; have the merger reject claims without evidence.
Send the same subtask to two workers and treat divergence as a stop condition.
Cap the chain at N=3 workers; beyond that the merge step's reliability falls off a cliff.

E_compliance.rationale: All workers and the merger typically run under one OAuth principal. Compliance frameworks expect role separation between executor and reviewer; this topology collapses that distinction into the merger.
conditions: Workers and merger share a single identity in the upstream system.
Workflow processes data subject to ISO 42001 or SOC 2 logical-access controls.
mitigations: Run workers under distinct service-account identities; require the merger to authenticate separately.
Log every worker → merger payload to an immutable audit store keyed by worker_id.
Document the principal-collapse explicitly in the workflow's compliance attestation.
